planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained aroid mix; give it a moss pole or slab early so the ridged, sculptural foliage develops its full climbing form.

directions: Pot this appressed climber in a coarse, fast-draining aroid blend and provide a rough vertical surface for its aerial roots to grip. Keep humidity high and let the top inch of substrate dry between waterings to avoid root rot. As the vine matures on its support, the deeply grooved, wing-petioled leaves become noticeably more textured and dramatic than in juvenile growth. Feed lightly during the active growing months to sustain steady new leaf production.

planting.note: Best grown in a high-humidity terrarium or vivarium setup with bright, filtered light and a chunky aroid mix; a small trellis lets the narrow, deeply lobed leaves display fully.

directions: Site this climber where humidity stays consistently high, such as an enclosed cabinet or glass terrarium, since dry air causes the fine leaf lobes to brown at the tips. Juvenile leaves start out simple and heart-shaped, then gradually mature into the intricately pinnate, feather-like form the species is prized for. Use a small-diameter pole or cork slab to support upward growth and keep the foliage from tangling on itself. Water when the top layer of mix begins to dry, avoiding prolonged soggy conditions.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or greenhouse climber in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained aroid mix; mature specimens occasionally reward growers with fragrant blooms.

directions: Provide a sturdy, rough-surfaced pole so this root-climbing species can attach and produce its characteristically short internodes and D-shaped petioles. Keep the reddish-brown fibrous cataphylls intact rather than stripping them off, since they protect emerging leaves. Grow in warm, humid conditions with consistent but not waterlogged moisture, letting the surface dry slightly between waterings. Given enough light and age, this species can produce highly fragrant flowers, a trait uncommon among cultivated aroid houseplants.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained aroid mix; its whorled, star-shaped leaflets look best displayed as a solitary specimen rather than crowded among other plants.

directions: Unlike most vining philodendrons, this species holds a self-heading, scrambling habit with leaves divided into ten or more narrow, radiating leaflets around a central hub. Pot it in a coarse, acidic aroid mix that drains quickly, and let the top of the substrate dry out somewhat between waterings. Bright, indirect light keeps the leaflet whorls tight and symmetrical, while low light causes leggy, sparse growth. Rotate the pot occasionally so the fan-like foliage develops evenly on all sides.

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in bright, indirect light in a chunky, well-drained aroid mix; give it a moss pole so the fuzzy, scale-covered petioles can be appreciated up close.

directions: This fast-growing hemiepiphyte is easy to identify by the dense, reddish scales covering its petioles, which fade toward a dried-blood color with age. Leaves are quilted and bicolor, glossy deep green above and silvery beneath, creating strong contrast as the plant climbs. Provide a rough support and consistently high humidity, since the textured petioles and cataphylls are prone to drying out in low-humidity indoor air. Water when the top of the mix has dried slightly, and feed during the growing season to encourage steady climbing growth.
